content: Children diagnosed with Tetralogy of Fallot may experience sudden episodes of severe cyanosis or hypoxic events, commonly referred to as Tet spells or hypercyanotic spells. These episodes are unpredictable and are characterized by profound cyanosis, which can be life-threatening. The exact mechanism behind Tet spells is not fully understood. However, it is believed that these episodes may result from a spasm of the infundibular septum and the right ventricular outflow tract. This leads to increased resistance to blood flow to the lungs and a preferential diversion of desaturated blood into the systemic circulation. During these episodes, children often instinctively squat, which enhances venous return to the right side of the heart. Squatting also increases systemic vascular resistance, redirecting blood flow to the pulmonary circuit and improving oxygenation. Diagnosis Symptoms: Prolonged episodes of crying may precede a Tet spell. Physical Examination: Vitals: Tachypnea (rapid breathing) is commonly observed. Skin: Intense cyanosis is a hallmark feature. Heart: The typically harsh murmur associated with Tetralogy of Fallot may become significantly diminished during a Tet spell due to reduced blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature. Emergency Medical Management of Tet Spells Tet spells result in acute hypoxia and require prompt intervention. Treatment options include: 1. Beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol or esmolol): These medications relax the right ventricular outflow tract, facilitating increased blood flow into the pulmonary vessels. 2. Morphine: Administered to reduce the ventilatory drive and calm the child, which can help alleviate the spell. 3. Phenylephrine: This medication increases systemic afterload, which promotes blood flow across the right ventricle and pulmonary artery while reducing right-to-left shunting. 4. Dexmedetomidine: Although evidence is limited to case reports, this medication has been used at a dose of 1–2.5 mcg/kg/hour (without a bolus) to manage Tet spells. 5. Knee-chest position: This maneuver increases aortic wave reflection, raising pressure on the left side of the heart. This reduces the right-to-left shunt and decreases the amount of deoxygenated blood entering systemic circulation. 6. Oxygen therapy: While oxygen is often administered, it is generally ineffective in treating hypoxic spells because the primary issue is reduced blood flow through the pulmonary circuit rather than inadequate alveolar oxygenation. 7. Blalock-Taussig shunt: In cases where all other measures fail, an emergency surgical procedure such as a Blalock-Taussig shunt may be necessary to improve pulmonary blood flow. 8. General anesthesia: This may be considered in certain situations to stabilize the patient. Prognosis Tet spells can be fatal if not promptly managed. Importantly, these episodes can occur even in patients who are not chronically cyanotic.
